chunks: "Multiphase improves transient response in two ways. The first is the inductor slew rate.
When the load steps up, the output capacitor supplies the difference until the inductor current catches up, and the inductor current can only rise at V in minus V out over L.
With N phases pushing at the same time, the total current rises N times faster, equivalent to a single inductor of L over N.
So the capacitor has to cover a much shorter gap and the droop is smaller. The second is control bandwidth.
The loop crossover is limited to a fraction of the switching frequency because the converter samples the output once per cycle.
With interleaving, the effective frequency is N times f sw, so the loop can have a higher crossover, and respond faster, without making each FET switch faster. Those two combine.
For a 12 volts to 1 volts rail with a 30 amp step, going from one phase to four cuts the ideal droop by about four times, so I can use around a quarter of the capacitance for the same limit.

The caveats: capacitor ESR and ESL add their own immediate step that no converter speed can fix; the unload step is slower than the load step because the down-slew is just V out over L, which is small at 1 volt; and when phases are shed at light load the response is slower unless the controller brings them back instantly."
